pages.text: The school bus rattled along a red road, and the class piled out in a village. “Welcome to Boabeng and Fiema,” said Mr Darkwah, the community guide. “Two villages beside one forest, and a forest beside two villages. Please walk gently, and do not offer food to the monkeys.” Silas looked up. In the trees above, black-and-white monkeys were leaping from branch to branch, calm as villagers on a market day.
sentences: The school bus rattled along a red road, and the class piled out in a village.
“Welcome to Boabeng and Fiema,” said Mr Darkwah, the community guide.
“Two villages beside one forest, and a forest beside two villages.
Please walk gently, and do not offer food to the monkeys.” Silas looked up.
In the trees above, black-and-white monkeys were leaping from branch to branch, calm as villagers on a market day.
pages.alt: Students step from a bus into a village while monkeys move through the trees overhead.

pages.text: “The villagers here,” said Mr Darkwah, “have long believed that the monkeys are sacred. For generations, nobody has been allowed to harm them, and the belief is passed from parents to children. When a monkey dies, it is buried in a small coffin, with respect and with rites, like a member of the community.” Silas wrote it down. “A funeral for a monkey,” he whispered.
sentences: “The villagers here,” said Mr Darkwah, “have long believed that the monkeys are sacred.
For generations, nobody has been allowed to harm them, and the belief is passed from parents to children.
When a monkey dies, it is buried in a small coffin, with respect and with rites, like a member of the community.” Silas wrote it down.
“A funeral for a monkey,” he whispered.
pages.alt: A guide points to a small wooden coffin beside a grave marker under a tree.

pages.text: “The forest here is small, only about two square kilometres, a sanctuary of 192 hectares inside a larger sacred grove of about four and a half,” said Mr Darkwah, “but the animals have been safe in it because the community protects it. Estimates for the sanctuary run from about six hundred to over seven hundred monkeys, and counts change from year to year. The two main kinds are the white-thighed colobus, which some books call Geoffroy’s pied colobus, and Campbell’s mona monkey. The colobus is critically endangered, yet researchers say this may be the only growing population of its kind in West Africa. Counts for 2006 differ between studies, from about 241 to over 365, so nobody here can give a firm number today.” Silas wrote in his notebook: forest small, monkeys many, community the guard.

Counts for 2006 differ between studies, from about 241 to over 365, so nobody here can give a firm number today.” Silas wrote in his notebook: forest small, monkeys many, community the guard.
pages.alt: A guide points to a map of a small forest patch surrounded by farms and houses.

pages.text: Madam Blay added, “This is called traditional conservation, which is protecting nature through custom and belief, rather than only through laws. Researchers have studied this sanctuary as an example. The belief protects the animals, and the animals, in turn, help the forest, because monkeys eat fruits and spread seeds as they travel.” Silas frowned. “Is the belief true, or is it just a story?” he asked.

The belief protects the animals, and the animals, in turn, help the forest, because monkeys eat fruits and spread seeds as they travel.” Silas frowned.
“Is the belief true, or is it just a story?” he asked.
pages.alt: A teacher stands beside a diagram of a monkey eating fruit and seeds falling to the forest floor.

pages.text: Mr Darkwah did not mind the question. “Some beliefs are about the spirit, and those I leave to our elders,” he said. “But whatever one believes about spirits, the monkeys protected by this custom are alive today, and the forest is standing. A custom can be a strong conservation tool, and a scientist can count and study. The best protection is when both listen to each other.”

The best protection is when both listen to each other.”
pages.alt: A guide and a boy talk while a monkey sits on a branch above them.

pages.text: But Mr Darkwah was honest about the problems. “When visitors or villagers feed the monkeys, they start to expect it, and that causes conflict over food. The roads are poor, so fewer visitors come, and the community earns less from tourism. And the forest is surrounded by farms, so it cannot grow.” He looked at the students. “The old way needs new help: better roads, fair tourism money and children who understand why this forest matters.”

“The old way needs new help: better roads, fair tourism money and children who understand why this forest matters.”
pages.alt: A guide points to a poor road, a farm boundary and a monkey on a roof as examples of problems.

pages.text: Silas did not feed a single monkey. When he stood under a tall tree, a young mona monkey dropped from a branch and watched him from a distance. “It is looking at me,” he whispered. “Only watch,” said Mr Darkwah, smiling. “That is how we say hello here.” Silas watched until the monkey leaped away, and he felt as though he had been introduced to the forest.

pages.alt: A boy stands still under a tree as a young monkey watches him from a low branch.

pages.text: On the bus ride home, Silas wrote a narrative. “‘Please walk gently,’ said Mr Darkwah as we entered the forest. ‘The monkeys were here long before us.’ I nodded and kept my voice low. High above, a monkey leaped across the branches. ‘They look like they own the place,’ whispered my friend. ‘They do,’ said Mr Darkwah, smiling, ‘and we are only guests.’”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: in direct speech, put the spoken words inside quotation marks, begin each speaker’s words with a capital letter, put the comma or full stop inside the closing quotation mark and start a new line for each new speaker. Silas wrote “said Mr Darkwah” after the words and kept the tense in the past. Check every quotation mark before you hand in your narrative. The end.
